title: Summit of a Single Mountain
statement:
An array arr is shaped like one mountain: its values strictly rise up to a single highest element, then strictly fall to the end. The summit is never the first or the last element.

Return the index of the summit. Your solution should take O(log n) time.

examples.why: The values climb to 8 at index 2, then drop.
The summit can sit right after the start. A search that only looks at the middle value would see 5 and stop on the wrong side if it does not compare with a neighbour.
A long climb and a short descent: the summit is near the end.

hints: A linear scan finds the first drop. But the array is not sorted, so what can you compare to decide which half holds the summit?
Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1]. If the next value is bigger, you are on the rising slope.
On the rising slope the summit is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left. Keep the half that contains it until one index remains.

explain.intuition:
The array is not sorted, but each position answers one yes/no question: is the next value higher? Every index before the summit says yes, the summit and everything after it say no. That is a sorted run of answers, yes … yes no … no, and binary search finds the first no, which is the summit.

Comparing with the neighbour is the key move. The middle value alone tells you nothing, because the same height can appear on both slopes.
steps: If arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1], the summit is right of mid: lo = mid + 1.
Otherwise mid is the summit or on the falling slope: hi = mid.
pitfalls: Comparing arr[mid] with arr[lo] or arr[hi]. Heights on opposite slopes cannot be compared that way.
Using hi = mid − 1 in the falling case. Mid itself might be the summit.
Reading arr[mid + 1] when mid can be the last index. With lo < hi and a floor midpoint, it never is.

solutions.title: Walk until the first drop
solutions.idea: Scan from the left; the first index whose next value is smaller is the summit.

solutions.title: Binary search on the slope
solutions.idea: Whether arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1] tells you which slope mid is on. Keep the half that contains the summit.

followups: Find a target value in a mountain array using O(log n) reads. (Find the summit, then binary search each slope.)
The array has several peaks and you only need any one of them. Does the same comparison still work?
